parakeet: The burden should be on Christianity to demonstrate why claims preserved under conditions of power, coercion, and selective memory deserve to be trusted in the first place, because good reason does not suggest that an institution willing to create, preserve, defend, and benefit from false information, would somehow become uniquely honest when telling its own story. If the church could falsify documents to defend its authority, why assume it would never falsify, embellish, sanitize, or strategically preserve claims about its founders? If it could invent legal history, why assume it never shaped sacred history? If it could misattribute writings to apostles, why assume its leading cast and supporting crew are exactly who later traditions claim they are? If it could suppress dissenting voices, why assume the surviving story is the truest story rather than the winning story? That, my friends, is the problem with hiding behind consensus. In Christianity's case, consensus becomes especially suspicious because the archive itself was shaped by the institution being evaluated. The surviving record may not represent what was most true. It may represent what was most protected. It may represent what was most useful. It may represent what the church successfully preserved after centuries of controlling the documents, doctrine, and boundaries of legitimate belief. We don't have better evidence is not the same thing as the church's version is probably true. We've inherited this tradition is not the same thing as this tradition has been verified. Most scholars accept this as not the same thing as this claim has escaped the gravitational pull of Christian institutional power. So, no, Christianity should not get to hide behind consensus when the consensus itself may be downstream from coercion, preservation bias, forged authority, theological politics, and centuries of manufactured certainty. Outside of church preserved claims, what can actually be verified? And until the question is answered with evidence, independent of the institution that benefited from the story, Christianity's claims should not be granted the privilege of default trust. They should be treated as claims awaiting verification, not sacred history, not neutral scholarship, not consensus-protected truths. Given the record of the institution that preserved these claims, suspicion is not bias. Suspicion is the minimum standard of intellectual responsibility.
